Energy Costs

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Together with our country's leading scientific energy researchers we debunk the need for nuclear, and show the numbers government and Eskom SHOULD arrive at, if they were being honest with us.

Unique Selling Point:
This is a pivotal moment in SA’s history when this generation will make decisions on our energy future that will impact generations to come. Renewable energy sources are cheaper, cleaner, easier to decommission and does not create dangerous waste that needs to be stored forever. So why are we not jumping at it?

Government’s insistence that we need to build new nuclear and coal-fired power stations to supply SA with the power we need is based on outdated data. And new research by the CSIR proves this. We are still operating on the assumptions in the Integrated Resource Plan on energy of 2010. Since then, the cost of solar PV panels and wind turbine technology has drastically fallen. Also, energy consumption has decreased.

We must ask the government why it has not created an updated IRP with updated data and released it for comment. Why has it not removed the new-build limits on renewable energy sources? Why is it insisting on forging ahead with expensive nuclear power plants instead of taking another look at the data it based its plans on?



Summary:
A new 2016 IRP has been prepared but is not yet released for public comment. This was recently delayed indefinitely – possibly because the ministerial advisory committee told the minister that renewable energy is the way to go rather than nuclear and new coal.

The CSIR has used the exact same model the DoE uses to generate the IRP to generate a revised energy plan for SA based on current data. They only changed one thing – removed the annual limit on building wind and solar power plants. It is unclear why this annual limit was included in the 2010 IRP. With this limit in place, renewable energy sources will never be a significant part of SA’s energy mix and we will need nuclear and coal power.

But with this limit removed, the CSIR’s re-optimised energy plan shows that the most cost-effective plan for SA is to have 70% renewable energy sources by 2040. If this plan is implemented, we will be generating more energy at a lower cost.

The CSIR is in the process of making their whole campus in Pretoria, and others around the country, energy independent. They are doing all sorts of interesting research to ascertain the best and most cost-effective ways to generate power.

Countries like China, India and Germany are taking up renewable energy and experience in those and other countries have shown that the renewable energy sector also creates jobs, instead of destroying them as some have warned. It also makes economic sense – the money from the power sector will be more widely distributed across the country too.

But in all cases, it is clear that energy transitions start from the top – political will and decisions from policy makers are required. Government says it is committed to renewable energy but yet it has not proven this by scratching the annual new-build limits on renewable energy sources.

Press Release:


Today’s decisions on South Africa's future electricity supply will impact the country for generations to come. Coal, solar, wind, gas or nuclear? How much of each and at what cost? Eskom and government remain committed to a hotly contested and very expensive nuclear build program, but leading energy experts have challenged the recently announced plan. Carte Blanche examines government's energy ambitions.

Script:


VO: Globally, the demand for electricity is increasing, but the fear of climate change has people demanding cleaner energy sources. South Africa is no exception. Our power consumption is predicted to double in the next 30 years or so. As our coal power stations age, the Department of Energy, or DOE, must decide where our electricity will come from in the future.

LINK DEVI: The Department of Energy has released their draft energy plan for the next 30 years. But experts argue that, based purely on the numbers, the plan doesn’t make sense.

VO: Ompi Aphane is the man who must show the department’s newly devised plan to the public in country-wide roadshows.

UPS OMPI: We have a program to try and take this energy planning process to all the corners of this country.

VO: Brenda Martin, chairperson of the South African Renewable Energy Council, attended one of these roadshows.

BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Comments that are coming through are so consistent. What are the assumptions that have been made? Why is it that nuclear has been moved forward in the current version update?

VO: Aphane, the deputy director-general in charge of policy, planning and clean energy in the DOE, says they will consider all input.

OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: We would have solicited input in relation to the assumptions, in relation to the scenarios...at the point where we have balanced the scenarios and we’re ready to submit to cabinet, we’ll go back to the public.

VO: The energy mix the DOE proposes by 2050 includes 30% nuclear power, 31% from coal and 23% from wind and solar. The plan comes five years after the previous version - five years during which progress has made power derived from the sun and wind the cheapest, cleanest and fastest to produce.

TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: With nuclear you historically had the cheapest carbon-free source of electricity. ...I talk like literally five to ten years ago. That has now flipped, we are now beyond the tipping point where the cheapest source of carbon-free electricity is not nuclear anymore but it’s now solar photovoltaic and wind.

VO: It was political will and investment in renewables that drove down costs the world over. Germany, Europe’s economic powerhouse, sets the example with its energy transition. In five years’ time it will have dismantled all its nuclear reactors and most of its power will come from the sun and wind. Renewable energy already supplies 34% of that country’s power and has created three hundred and seventy thousand jobs. China is building new nuclear plants, but also adding twice as much in renewables. Back home, Dr Tobias Bischof-Niemz explains that the DOE’s plan is generated by a computer modelling program called Plexos, which is used by power system planners the world over. But what you get out depends on what you put in - and the DOE placed an annual limit on new renewable energy as a starting point.

TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: The model builds the cheapest form of electricity supply first, and that is wind and solar PV, and it builds that up to the limit that is allowed by the constraints put in place. Then it goes to the second cheapest, which is coal, and it builds coal up to the carbon limit...And once no more carbon emissions are allowed, then it goes to the third cheapest option, which is nuclear.

VO: Bischof-Niemz heads the Energy Centre at the country’s scientific think tank, the CSIR. He and his colleagues used the same software to come up with an alternative electricity plan.

TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: The only material change that we did was to lift constraints that were imposed on renewables, namely solar PV and wind. If you lift the constraints on renewables, the model builds almost exclusively renewables.

VO: This model looks very different from government’s draft. Renewables make up 70% of the mix by 2050 and there’s no new nuclear needed.

LINK DEVI: Government says it’s committed to renewable energy. Yet there is a cap on the amount of renewable energy that can be added every year.

VO: The DOE says the limits on new renewables are needed, because in some areas the grid is maxed out.

OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: The grid in the Northern Cape, which is where the best solar resource prevails, is already constrained.

VO: Grid upgrades are required before more power can be fed in, but the DOE is not in charge of the grid, says Aphane, the deputy director-general in charge of policy, planning and clean energy in the DOE. The grid belongs to Eskom.

OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: What we then do, is we encourage the grid to be upgraded.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: I produce electricity - solar, wind, whatever. Is there a problem with me feeding that back into the grid?
BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: The problem is really that ESKOM is going to lose revenue.

VO: Meanwhile, Eskom’s nuclear drive gains momentum. Last month, Energy Minister Tina Joemat-Pettersson designated Eskom the nuclear procurer, giving it the green light for 9.6 gigawatt of new nuclear. This, despite its dismal track record in delivering new build on time and on budget.

LINK DEVI: Since the end of November 2016, we’ve made numerous requests asking Eskom for an on-camera interview. To date, we have no interview.

VO: While Interim Group CEO Eskom Matshela Koko would neither speak to us, nor delegate a spokesman, he airs his views on Twitter. On 31 December, shortly after the Kusile coal power station started producing electricity, he wished his followers a happy new year and wrote that there would be power, even if the sun and wind failed. In the past week, he called the CSIR a lobby group for renewable energy. The CSIR Energy Centre backs its science up with real-world tests. It produces solar energy on site to power its Pretoria campus and hopes to feed surplus back into Tshwane’s grid. Sengiphile Simelane ensures efficient output.

SENGIPHILE SIMELANE, CSIR ENERGY CENTRE ENGINEER: How it works is that it’s got some sensor that senses the optimum position of the sun and it will always position itself in that particular direction.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: It actually moves?

SENGIPHILE SIMELANE: It moves, yes.

VO: These modern solar photovoltaic panels are a far cry from those at solar entrepreneur Gareth Warner’s RustMo One plant near Rustenburg, the first solar farm to start selling power to Eskom three years ago.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: If you had to build this farm now, what would it cost?
GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: It’d probably cost us almost 50% less.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: That much?
GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: The prices of the modules have come down significantly, and the build cost, because the industry has matured in South Africa. When we developed this solar farm there was actually no companies in the country that could build it, so we used in this case German engineering, combined with some South African build expertise.

VO: His plant is part of the government’s revolutionary and successful independent power producer program for renewable energy that started in 2010 in the wake of loadshedding woes.

GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: This was one of the leading programmes in the world. I did work in the UK for a few years and if I compare the programme there and in some other European countries to South Africa, we have a very advanced and very competitive programme.

DEVI LINK: But there’s now a delay. The preferred suppliers are in limbo. They haven’t been given the go-ahead by Eskom and the Department of Energy.

VO: Now that loadshedding’s been addressed and Eskom’s new coal power stations Medupi and Kusile are open for business, it seems Eskom no longer wants to pay new independent producers for renewable power. Energy analyst Chris Yelland.

CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: Eskom is conflicted. On the one hand, it has got its own generation capacity. It also owns the national grid and it decides who it’s going to connect and who it’s not going to connect. And in times of a surplus, as we are entering into now, it naturally wants to operate its own plant preferentially.

VO: In the latest round of the program, the price for wind and solar power is 62 cents per kilowatt/hour -- two rand cheaper than in round one. But the contracts remain unsigned. Aphane says Eskom is in a corner.

OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: They plan, they build, they produce and they sell. So they have, you know, full control of the value chain … Now, there’s so much of the energy that is coming through the pipeline, and as it increases … the impact on its operations, the impact on its balance sheet, on their own, you know, aspirations ... it would change, it would be affected.

VO: The South African Renewable Energy Council is threatening court action over the 20-month impasse.

BRENDA MARTIN: CHAIR: SOUTH AFRICAN RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: We had 32 000 jobs created by that point. With the delay the on power purchase agreements we are at risk of losing 15 000 jobs.

VO: But on Friday, Eskom promised it would soon have a solution. On the nuclear build front, Eskom has asked possible partners for information, though tendering can’t start without Treasury’s approval. The programme could cost up to a trillion rand, with speculation that Russia’s state nuclear corporation ROSATOM is a preferred partner. New nuclear is set to go live by 2026. The DOE’s plan could mean 25 gigawatt of nuclear for South Africa.

TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: A 20 GW nuclear fleet is one of the largest nuclear fleets that the world has seen so far. Now, to put this into perspective, a 30% energy share coming from nuclear, there’s less than a handful of countries that has that today.

BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Eskom is determined to procure nuclear. I don’t know on what basis it believes it will make money with nuclear power because the numbers just don’t make any sense.

CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: We should not mortgage our future for the next 100 years into a particular technology in an uncertain world where technology is changing. So I would proceed cautiously, step by step, and not make massive commitments.

LINK DEVI: This is not a pro- or anti-nuclear argument. This is about what is best for South Africa for generations to come.

CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: The decisions that are taken in this planning document are such that it will affect our children and even our children’s children.

TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: We basically have to decide how do we rebuild the entire South African power system in the next 35 years. And that decision has to be taken today.

VO: The numbers speak for themselves. Nuclear - according to favourable Russian estimates - comes in at R1,17 per kilowatt/hour; coal about R1 and wind and solar PV…62c. According to the CSIR’s calculations, it would be ninety billion rand a year cheaper by 2050 to run the power system in their least cost model than in the DOE’s plan.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: That’s a lot.
TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: Not once-off, it’s per year.

VO: But there may be other considerations.

CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: It’s not just about costs, it’s about managing risk. You may be prepared to pay a premium at the moment in order to achieve other objectives.

VO: Other objectives, like making sure there’s never an outage, whatever the weather. But experts - and the computer model - prefer gas and new technologies, like concentrated solar power that stores energy in salt for use on demand. Though now pricey, economies of scale will drive cost down. In fact, our first CSP plants are operational in the Northern Cape.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Are you for mixed resources?
BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Yes, I am …
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: So you’re not saying you’re against nuclear?
BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: No, I am for power that doesn’t come with risks and that doesn’t come with poor transparency, poor governance and that makes it impossible to shift when you need to.

VO: The public has until the end of March to comment on the DOE’s plan, with roadshows still planned in five cities.

Coal, solar, wind, gas or nuclear? How much of each and at what cost? Eskom and government remain committed to a hotly contested and very expensive nuclear build program, but leading energy experts have challenged the recently announced plan. Carte Blanche examines government's energy ambitions. Script: VO: Globally, the demand for electricity is increasing, but the fear of climate change has people demanding cleaner energy sources. South Africa is no exception. Our power consumption is predicted to double in the next 30 years or so. As our coal power stations age, the Department of Energy, or DOE, must decide where our electricity will come from in the future. LINK DEVI: The Department of Energy has released their draft energy plan for the next 30 years. But experts argue that, based purely on the numbers, the plan doesn’t make sense. VO: Ompi Aphane is the man who must show the department’s newly devised plan to the public in country-wide roadshows. UPS OMPI: We have a program to try and take this energy planning process to all the corners of this country. VO: Brenda Martin, chairperson of the South African Renewable Energy Council, attended one of these roadshows. BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Comments that are coming through are so consistent. What are the assumptions that have been made? Why is it that nuclear has been moved forward in the current version update? VO: Aphane, the deputy director-general in charge of policy, planning and clean energy in the DOE, says they will consider all input. OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: We would have solicited input in relation to the assumptions, in relation to the scenarios...at the point where we have balanced the scenarios and we’re ready to submit to cabinet, we’ll go back to the public. VO: The energy mix the DOE proposes by 2050 includes 30% nuclear power, 31% from coal and 23% from wind and solar. The plan comes five years after the previous version - five years during which progress has made power derived from the sun and wind the cheapest, cleanest and fastest to produce. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: With nuclear you historically had the cheapest carbon-free source of electricity. ...I talk like literally five to ten years ago. That has now flipped, we are now beyond the tipping point where the cheapest source of carbon-free electricity is not nuclear anymore but it’s now solar photovoltaic and wind. VO: It was political will and investment in renewables that drove down costs the world over. Germany, Europe’s economic powerhouse, sets the example with its energy transition. In five years’ time it will have dismantled all its nuclear reactors and most of its power will come from the sun and wind. Renewable energy already supplies 34% of that country’s power and has created three hundred and seventy thousand jobs. China is building new nuclear plants, but also adding twice as much in renewables. Back home, Dr Tobias Bischof-Niemz explains that the DOE’s plan is generated by a computer modelling program called Plexos, which is used by power system planners the world over. But what you get out depends on what you put in - and the DOE placed an annual limit on new renewable energy as a starting point. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: The model builds the cheapest form of electricity supply first, and that is wind and solar PV, and it builds that up to the limit that is allowed by the constraints put in place. Then it goes to the second cheapest, which is coal, and it builds coal up to the carbon limit...And once no more carbon emissions are allowed, then it goes to the third cheapest option, which is nuclear. VO: Bischof-Niemz heads the Energy Centre at the country’s scientific think tank, the CSIR. He and his colleagues used the same software to come up with an alternative electricity plan. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: The only material change that we did was to lift constraints that were imposed on renewables, namely solar PV and wind. If you lift the constraints on renewables, the model builds almost exclusively renewables. VO: This model looks very different from government’s draft. Renewables make up 70% of the mix by 2050 and there’s no new nuclear needed. LINK DEVI: Government says it’s committed to renewable energy. Yet there is a cap on the amount of renewable energy that can be added every year. VO: The DOE says the limits on new renewables are needed, because in some areas the grid is maxed out. OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: The grid in the Northern Cape, which is where the best solar resource prevails, is already constrained. VO: Grid upgrades are required before more power can be fed in, but the DOE is not in charge of the grid, says Aphane, the deputy director-general in charge of policy, planning and clean energy in the DOE. The grid belongs to Eskom. OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: What we then do, is we encourage the grid to be upgraded. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: I produce electricity - solar, wind, whatever. Is there a problem with me feeding that back into the grid? BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: The problem is really that ESKOM is going to lose revenue. VO: Meanwhile, Eskom’s nuclear drive gains momentum. Last month, Energy Minister Tina Joemat-Pettersson designated Eskom the nuclear procurer, giving it the green light for 9.6 gigawatt of new nuclear. This, despite its dismal track record in delivering new build on time and on budget. LINK DEVI: Since the end of November 2016, we’ve made numerous requests asking Eskom for an on-camera interview. To date, we have no interview. VO: While Interim Group CEO Eskom Matshela Koko would neither speak to us, nor delegate a spokesman, he airs his views on Twitter. On 31 December, shortly after the Kusile coal power station started producing electricity, he wished his followers a happy new year and wrote that there would be power, even if the sun and wind failed. In the past week, he called the CSIR a lobby group for renewable energy. The CSIR Energy Centre backs its science up with real-world tests. It produces solar energy on site to power its Pretoria campus and hopes to feed surplus back into Tshwane’s grid. Sengiphile Simelane ensures efficient output. SENGIPHILE SIMELANE, CSIR ENERGY CENTRE ENGINEER: How it works is that it’s got some sensor that senses the optimum position of the sun and it will always position itself in that particular direction. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: It actually moves? SENGIPHILE SIMELANE: It moves, yes. VO: These modern solar photovoltaic panels are a far cry from those at solar entrepreneur Gareth Warner’s RustMo One plant near Rustenburg, the first solar farm to start selling power to Eskom three years ago. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: If you had to build this farm now, what would it cost? GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: It’d probably cost us almost 50% less. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: That much? GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: The prices of the modules have come down significantly, and the build cost, because the industry has matured in South Africa. When we developed this solar farm there was actually no companies in the country that could build it, so we used in this case German engineering, combined with some South African build expertise. VO: His plant is part of the government’s revolutionary and successful independent power producer program for renewable energy that started in 2010 in the wake of loadshedding woes. GARETH WARNER, MANAGING DIRECTOR: MOMENTOUS ENERGY: This was one of the leading programmes in the world. I did work in the UK for a few years and if I compare the programme there and in some other European countries to South Africa, we have a very advanced and very competitive programme. DEVI LINK: But there’s now a delay. The preferred suppliers are in limbo. They haven’t been given the go-ahead by Eskom and the Department of Energy. VO: Now that loadshedding’s been addressed and Eskom’s new coal power stations Medupi and Kusile are open for business, it seems Eskom no longer wants to pay new independent producers for renewable power. Energy analyst Chris Yelland. CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: Eskom is conflicted. On the one hand, it has got its own generation capacity. It also owns the national grid and it decides who it’s going to connect and who it’s not going to connect. And in times of a surplus, as we are entering into now, it naturally wants to operate its own plant preferentially. VO: In the latest round of the program, the price for wind and solar power is 62 cents per kilowatt/hour -- two rand cheaper than in round one. But the contracts remain unsigned. Aphane says Eskom is in a corner. OMPI APHANE, DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY: They plan, they build, they produce and they sell. So they have, you know, full control of the value chain … Now, there’s so much of the energy that is coming through the pipeline, and as it increases … the impact on its operations, the impact on its balance sheet, on their own, you know, aspirations ... it would change, it would be affected. VO: The South African Renewable Energy Council is threatening court action over the 20-month impasse. BRENDA MARTIN: CHAIR: SOUTH AFRICAN RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: We had 32 000 jobs created by that point. With the delay the on power purchase agreements we are at risk of losing 15 000 jobs. VO: But on Friday, Eskom promised it would soon have a solution. On the nuclear build front, Eskom has asked possible partners for information, though tendering can’t start without Treasury’s approval. The programme could cost up to a trillion rand, with speculation that Russia’s state nuclear corporation ROSATOM is a preferred partner. New nuclear is set to go live by 2026. The DOE’s plan could mean 25 gigawatt of nuclear for South Africa. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: A 20 GW nuclear fleet is one of the largest nuclear fleets that the world has seen so far. Now, to put this into perspective, a 30% energy share coming from nuclear, there’s less than a handful of countries that has that today. BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Eskom is determined to procure nuclear. I don’t know on what basis it believes it will make money with nuclear power because the numbers just don’t make any sense. CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: We should not mortgage our future for the next 100 years into a particular technology in an uncertain world where technology is changing. So I would proceed cautiously, step by step, and not make massive commitments. LINK DEVI: This is not a pro- or anti-nuclear argument. This is about what is best for South Africa for generations to come. CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: The decisions that are taken in this planning document are such that it will affect our children and even our children’s children. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: We basically have to decide how do we rebuild the entire South African power system in the next 35 years. And that decision has to be taken today. VO: The numbers speak for themselves. Nuclear - according to favourable Russian estimates - comes in at R1,17 per kilowatt/hour; coal about R1 and wind and solar PV…62c. According to the CSIR’s calculations, it would be ninety billion rand a year cheaper by 2050 to run the power system in their least cost model than in the DOE’s plan. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: That’s a lot. TOBIAS BISCHOF-NIEMZ, HEAD: CSIR ENERGY CENTRE: Not once-off, it’s per year. VO: But there may be other considerations. CHRIS YELLAND, INDEPENDENT ENERGY ANALYST: It’s not just about costs, it’s about managing risk. You may be prepared to pay a premium at the moment in order to achieve other objectives. VO: Other objectives, like making sure there’s never an outage, whatever the weather. But experts - and the computer model - prefer gas and new technologies, like concentrated solar power that stores energy in salt for use on demand. Though now pricey, economies of scale will drive cost down. In fact, our first CSP plants are operational in the Northern Cape. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Are you for mixed resources? BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: Yes, I am … DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: So you’re not saying you’re against nuclear? BRENDA MARTIN, CHAIR: SA RENEWABLE ENERGY COUNCIL: No, I am for power that doesn’t come with risks and that doesn’t come with poor transparency, poor governance and that makes it impossible to shift when you need to. VO: The public has until the end of March to comment on the DOE’s plan, with roadshows still planned in five cities.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Together with our country's leading scientific energy researchers we debunk the need for nuclear, and show the numbers government and Eskom SHOULD arrive at, if they were being honest with us.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a pivotal moment in SA’s history when this generation will make decisions on our energy future that will impact generations to come. Renewable energy sources are cheaper, cleaner, easier to decommission and does not create dangerous waste that needs to be stored forever. So why are we not jumping at it? Government’s insistence that we need to build new nuclear and coal-fired power stations to supply SA with the power we need is based on outdated data. And new research by the CSIR proves this. We are still operating on the assumptions in the Integrated Resource Plan on energy of 2010. Since then, the cost of solar PV panels and wind turbine technology has drastically fallen. Also, energy consumption has decreased. We must ask the government why it has not created an updated IRP with updated data and released it for comment. Why has it not removed the new-build limits on renewable energy sources? Why is it insisting on forging ahead with expensive nuclear power plants instead of taking another look at the data it based its plans on?
metadata.Summary: A new 2016 IRP has been prepared but is not yet released for public comment. This was recently delayed indefinitely – possibly because the ministerial advisory committee told the minister that renewable energy is the way to go rather than nuclear and new coal. The CSIR has used the exact same model the DoE uses to generate the IRP to generate a revised energy plan for SA based on current data. They only changed one thing – removed the annual limit on building wind and solar power plants. It is unclear why this annual limit was included in the 2010 IRP. With this limit in place, renewable energy sources will never be a significant part of SA’s energy mix and we will need nuclear and coal power. But with this limit removed, the CSIR’s re-optimised energy plan shows that the most cost-effective plan for SA is to have 70% renewable energy sources by 2040. If this plan is implemented, we will be generating more energy at a lower cost. The CSIR is in the process of making their whole campus in Pretoria, and others around the country, energy independent. They are doing all sorts of interesting research to ascertain the best and most cost-effective ways to generate power. Countries like China, India and Germany are taking up renewable energy and experience in those and other countries have shown that the renewable energy sector also creates jobs, instead of destroying them as some have warned. It also makes economic sense – the money from the power sector will be more widely distributed across the country too. But in all cases, it is clear that energy transitions start from the top – political will and decisions from policy makers are required. Government says it is committed to renewable energy but yet it has not proven this by scratching the annual new-build limits on renewable energy sources.
